title: Readmitted to England
hook: Menasseh ben Israel petitions Cromwell, and Jews quietly return

segments.voice: Yesterday, Spinoza, cut off by his community and argued about ever since. Did you manage to say someone else's view back to them fairly? Today the week ends, and a door that had been shut for a long time begins to open. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

A few weeks ago on this path, a king ordered every Jew out of England. Homes emptied. A London street kept only the name, Old Jewry. Now a rabbi from Amsterdam is crossing the North Sea with a petition in his bag. He is a teacher, a writer and a printer, and he has a big hope and a practical request. He wants to ask England's ruler, Oliver Cromwell, a simple question: may we come back? Today, what answer he got.
screen: `ENGLAND'S DOOR, SHUT.` → `A RABBI FROM AMSTERDAM.` → `MAY WE COME BACK?`

segments.voice: His name was Menasseh ben Israel. He came from the Amsterdam community we met two days ago, and he carried two kinds of reasons. One was a hope. The Torah speaks of Israel scattered from one end of the earth to the other, and Menasseh wrote that the redemption would come once the scattering was complete. If Jews could live in England too, he believed, that day would come nearer. The other reason was plainer: Jews needed places to live safely, and they could bring trade and skill. He addressed Cromwell in writing, and later answered the old lies about Jews in a pamphlet of his own. Cromwell called a conference in London. Merchants, lawyers and clergy argued. Some wanted Jews admitted. Some wanted strict conditions. Some wanted no admission at all. And the meeting ended without a formal decision. No law was passed. No grand gate swung open. Menasseh was left disappointed. But something quieter happened. A small group of Jews was already living in London, living outwardly as Spanish and Portuguese Catholic merchants. They asked to pray together in private and to bury their dead, and they were allowed to. They rented a house for a synagogue and found land for a cemetery. That is what readmitted looks like here: not a ceremony, but a door left unlocked, and people walking through it carefully. Look back over this week. A tablecloth spread over a code of law. The lion of Safed. Mystics singing Lecha Dodi to greet Shabbat. Walls around the ghetto in Venice. A new home in Amsterdam. A son of that home cut off. And now, a door that had been shut opening a crack.
screen: `MENASSEH BEN ISRAEL'S PETITION.` · `A HOPE AND A PRACTICAL REQUEST.` · `A CONFERENCE WITH NO DECISION.` · `A DOOR LEFT UNLOCKED.` · then, large: `READMITTED.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: ask for a door to open. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Think of one door in your life that is closed: a relationship, a place, a chance you want. Menasseh asked in writing, plainly, and made his case. What would your request sound like if you said it plainly? Shape it in your mind in one or two sentences. You don't have to send it today. Just find the words. If you pray, you can bring that request in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Menasseh. The Amsterdam rabbi who petitioned Oliver Cromwell to let Jews return to England, and watched a door open quietly instead of by law. Today's word.
Your line: readmitted. Today, if a door has opened a crack for you, walk through it, even carefully. Or open one a crack for someone else. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish communities in Britain trace their modern history to this quiet return, and the Spanish and Portuguese congregation in London still keeps the customs of the families who came back.

fork.setup: you are Cromwell. merchants, lawyers and clergy have argued for days about letting Jews return. what do you do?
options: pass a law readmitting the Jews with full rights.
order the Jews in London to leave.
end the meeting without a formal decision.
fork.reveal: no law was passed. but the Jews already in London were quietly allowed to pray and bury their dead: readmitted without a ceremony.

trapdoor: what you thought: readmitted means a formal invitation back.
what it means: Jews returned to England through quiet permission to live, pray and bury their dead, not a grand law.
what a scholar hears: Menasseh linked the return to the scattering of Israel 'from one end of the earth' (Deuteronomy 28:64) and the hope of redemption.
